region: Mexico south of 23N, Central America, the Caribbean and South America: Native, maroon and mission polities 1400-1900

polities.name: Aztec Triple Alliance
polities.note: Hegemonic tributary empire of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan; extent = contiguous tributary provinces c.1519. Detached province of Xoconochco (Soconusco) listed separately. Enclaves not ruled: Tlaxcala, Huexotzinco, Metztitlan, Yopitzinco, Tututepec. Fell to Cortés 1521.

polities.name: Tepanec Empire
polities.note: Dominant power of the Basin of Mexico under Tezozomoc (d.1426); Mexica Tenochtitlan was its tributary until the 1428 war that created the Triple Alliance.

polities.name: Acolhua Texcoco
polities.note: Acolhua capital; subject to the Tepanecs 1418-1428, then partner in the Triple Alliance (draw under the Alliance 1428-1521 if needed).

polities.name: Chalco Confederation
polities.note: Independent altepetl confederation of the SE Basin of Mexico; conquered by the Mexica after a long war, 1465.

polities.name: Tlaxcala
polities.note: Confederation of four altepetl (Tepeticpac, Ocotelolco, Tizatlan, Quiahuiztlan) never conquered by the Aztecs; allied with Cortés 1519 and kept privileged self-government inside New Spain afterwards.

polities.name: Huexotzinco
polities.note: Independent Nahua altepetl east of the volcanoes; flower-war enemy of the Aztecs, allied with Spain 1519.

polities.name: Cholula
polities.note: Sacred Nahua city-state; oscillated between Tlaxcalan and Aztec alignment; massacre by Cortés 1519.

polities.name: Metztitlan
polities.note: Otomi/Nahua lordship in the Sierra of Hidalgo that resisted the Aztecs; submitted to the Spanish 1522-1530s.

polities.name: Yopitzinco
polities.note: Independent Yope/Tlapanec enclave on the Guerrero coast east of Acapulco, never conquered by the Aztecs.

polities.name: Matlatzinca
polities.note: Matlatzinca lordships of the Toluca valley conquered by Axayacatl c.1474-1478.

polities.name: Tarascan State
polities.note: Capital first Pátzcuaro, then Ihuatzio, then Tzintzuntzan (from c.1440s). Held the Aztec frontier on the Lerma/Balsas; submitted peacefully to Spain 1522, Cazonci Tangaxuan II executed 1530.

polities.name: Colima chiefdom
polities.note: Coliman lordship that fought the Tarascans in the Salitre war; conquered by Gonzalo de Sandoval 1523.

polities.name: Tonallan
polities.note: Lordship of central Jalisco ruled by a cihuapilli (queen) at the Spanish arrival; submitted to Nuño de Guzmán 1530.

polities.name: Caxcan
polities.note: Uto-Aztecan people of southern Zacatecas/northern Jalisco; led the Mixtón War 1540-1542, defeated at Nochistlán and Mixtón.

polities.name: Cora of Nayarit
polities.note: Independent Cora polity under the Nayarit lineage in the Sierra del Nayar until the Spanish conquest of the Mesa del Nayar in 1722; the Huichol held adjacent sierra land to the east.

polities.name: Wixárika (Huichol)
polities.note: Autonomous mountain communities east of the Cora; nominally under Spain after 1722 but largely self-governing into the 20th century.

polities.name: Guachichil
polities.note: Mobile Chichimec nation of the Tunal Grande (San Luis Potosí); fought the Chichimeca War 1550-1590, settled in missions after c.1590-1600. Extent clipped at 23N.

polities.name: Guamare and Pame
polities.note: Chichimec peoples of the Bajío and western Sierra Gorda, warring in the Chichimeca War 1550-1590.

polities.name: Sierra Gorda Jonaz
polities.note: Jonaz and Pame bands kept the Sierra Gorda independent until the campaigns of José de Escandón (Media Luna 1748).

polities.name: Huaxtec chiefdoms
polities.note: Many small Teenek lordships; southern towns (Tuxpan, Tziuhcoac) paid tribute to the Aztecs after c.1450-1480; conquered by Cortés 1522. Extent clipped at 23N.

polities.name: Totonacapan
polities.note: Totonac lordships headed by Cempoala; Aztec tributaries from the 1460s; allied with Cortés 1519.

polities.name: Tututepec
polities.note: Largest Mixtec kingdom, on the Oaxaca coast from the Guerrero border to Huatulco; never subjected by the Aztecs; conquered by Pedro de Alvarado 1522.

polities.name: Coixtlahuaca
polities.note: Chocho-Mixtec trading kingdom conquered by Moctezuma I in 1458 and made an Aztec tributary province.

polities.name: Tilantongo
polities.note: Senior Mixteca Alta dynasty of the codices; Aztec tributary in its last decades.

polities.name: Yanhuitlán
polities.note: Mixteca Alta lordship; Aztec tributary from the reign of Ahuitzotl; submitted to Spain c.1525.

polities.name: Tlaxiaco
polities.note: Mixteca Alta lordship (with Achiutla) conquered by Moctezuma II c.1511.

polities.name: Zaachila
polities.note: Main Zapotec royal seat of the Valley of Oaxaca; ruling house moved to Tehuantepec c.1490s; Aztec garrison at Huaxyacac from 1486; Mixtec Cuilapan inside the valley.

polities.name: Tehuantepec
polities.note: Zapotec kingdom of the Isthmus under Cocijoeza (resisted the Aztecs at Guiengola 1496) and Cocijopii, who submitted to Spain 1521 and ruled as cacique until 1563.

polities.name: Mixe
polities.note: Mountain people around Zempoaltépetl never subdued by the Aztecs; resisted Spanish campaigns until c.1570.

polities.name: Xoconochco
polities.note: Cacao-rich Pacific coast lordships; conquered by Ahuitzotl 1486 as a detached Aztec province; taken by Alvarado 1524.

polities.name: League of Mayapan
polities.note: Cocom-led confederation dominating northern Yucatán; destroyed in a Xiu-led revolt c.1441, after which some 16-17 provinces (kuchkabalob) emerged.

polities.name: Ah Canul
polities.note: Post-Mayapán province on the NW Yucatán coast; submitted to the Montejos 1541.

polities.name: Chakan
polities.note: Province without a single ruler (governed by Canche batabob); Mérida founded on Tiho 1542.

polities.name: Ceh Pech
polities.note: Pech lineage province on the north coast; allied with the Spanish.

polities.name: Ah Kin Chel
polities.note: Founded by Mo-Chel after Mayapán's fall; last ruler Namux Chel; conquered 1540s.

polities.name: Hocabá
polities.note: Small inland province between Chakan and Sotuta.

polities.name: Maní
polities.note: Xiu province; ruler Ah Kukum Xiu allied with Montejo the Younger 1541-1542.

polities.name: Sotuta
polities.note: Cocom province led by Nachi Cocom; central to the 1546-1547 Great Maya Revolt.

polities.name: Cupul
polities.note: Large eastern province including Chichén Itzá; rose in 1546-1547 revolt.

polities.name: Tases
polities.note: Small NE province between Cupul and Ecab.

polities.name: Chikinchel
polities.note: Salt-producing north coast province; seat location approximate.

polities.name: Ecab
polities.note: NE tip of Yucatán with several powerful batabob; first province seen by Spaniards (1517).

polities.name: Cozumel
polities.note: Island pilgrimage centre (Ix Chel) and province.

polities.name: Cochuah
polities.note: Eastern interior province; later the core of the 19th-century Caste War rebels.

polities.name: Uaymil
polities.note: Sparsely documented coastal province between Cochuah and Chetumal.

polities.name: Chetumal
polities.note: Cacao-rich province around Chetumal Bay where Gonzalo Guerrero lived; resisted Dávila 1531, subdued 1544.

polities.name: Chakan Putum
polities.note: Couoh lordship that defeated Hernández de Córdoba 1517; includes Canpech (Campeche) province to the north.

polities.name: Acalan
polities.note: Chontal (Putun) trading kingdom on the Candelaria river; ruler Paxbolonacha received Cortés 1525; moved to Tixchel 1557.

polities.name: Itza Kingdom
polities.note: Last independent Maya kingdom, ruled by the Kan Ekʼ dynasty from the island capital Nojpetén on Lake Petén Itzá; conquered by Martín de Ursúa 13 March 1697.

polities.name: Kowoj
polities.note: Rival of the Itza in the eastern Petén lakes; conquered 1697.

polities.name: Yalain
polities.note: Eastern Petén province, intermittently subject to the Itza.

polities.name: Kejache
polities.note: Maya people in the forest between Petén and Campeche; reduced in the 1695-1696 road campaign.

polities.name: Chʼol Lacandon
polities.note: Chʼol-speaking Lacandon of the Lacandon forest; island fortress of Lakam Tun destroyed 1586; later centre Sakbʼajlan taken 1695.

polities.name: Manche Chʼol
polities.note: Chʼol and Mopan communities of southern Belize/SE Petén; Dominican missions 1600s, deported to Verapaz c.1700.

polities.name: Kʼicheʼ Kingdom
polities.note: Dominant highland Maya kingdom; peaked under Kʼiqʼabʼ (d. c.1475) with conquests to the Pacific coast and Quetzaltenango; burnt by Alvarado 1524.

polities.name: Kaqchikel Kingdom
polities.note: Broke from the Kʼicheʼ c.1470; capital Iximche; allied with Alvarado 1524, revolted 1524-1530.

polities.name: Tzʼutujil Kingdom
polities.note: Lake Atitlán kingdom with cacao lands on the Pacific piedmont; defeated by Alvarado 1524.

polities.name: Mam Kingdom
polities.note: Mam capital Zaculeu fell to Gonzalo de Alvarado after a siege in 1525; subject to the Kʼicheʼ in the 15th century.

polities.name: Poqomam
polities.note: Poqomam (or Chajoma Kaqchikel) fortress-capital conquered 1525.

polities.name: Rabinal Achi
polities.note: Achi kingdom of the Rabinal basin, sometime Kʼicheʼ rival; absorbed into Dominican Verapaz from 1537.

polities.name: Tezulutlán
polities.note: Qʼeqchiʼ lordships that repelled Spanish conquest; brought under Spain by Dominican peaceful conversion 1537-1550 (renamed Verapaz).

polities.name: Uspantán
polities.note: Uspantek and Ixil polity that defeated a Spanish expedition 1529 before falling 1530.

polities.name: Zinacantan
polities.note: Tzotzil trading lordship of the Chiapas highlands; aided Spanish against Chiapa 1524.

polities.name: Chiapa
polities.note: Warlike Otomanguean kingdom of the central Grijalva depression; never subdued by the Aztecs; conquered by Diego de Mazariegos 1528.

polities.name: Chan Santa Cruz
aliases: Noj Kaj Santa Cruz Xbʼalam Naʼ
polities.note: Independent Maya theocratic state of the Caste War rebels (Talking Cross); held eastern Yucatán from Tulum to Bacalar (taken 1858); traded with British Honduras; capital occupied by Mexico 1901.

polities.name: Icaiché
polities.note: Southern Maya group that made peace with Mexico 1853 but ran its own affairs, raiding British Honduras (Marcos Canul) 1866-1872; absorbed after 1901.

polities.name: Cuzcatlan
polities.note: Nahua-speaking Pipil lordship of central El Salvador; resisted Alvarado 1524-1525 (Atlácatl); subdued by 1528, revolts to 1539.

polities.name: Izalco
polities.note: Western Pipil cacao lordship (Itzcalco), separate from Cuzcatlan.

polities.name: Copán Chʼortiʼ
polities.note: Chʼortiʼ Maya chiefdoms of the Copán valley; Copan Galel resisted the Spanish 1530.

polities.name: Lenca chiefdoms
polities.note: Lenca groups (Care, Cerquín, Potón, Guaquí) of western Honduras and eastern El Salvador; Lempira's confederacy fought the Spanish 1537-1539.

polities.name: Tolupan
polities.note: Unconquered forest people of Yoro and Olancho; outside colonial control until 19th-century reductions.

polities.name: Pech
polities.note: Chibchan people of NE Honduras; raided and tributary to the Miskito Kingdom in the 18th century.

polities.name: Nicarao
polities.note: Nahua chiefdom on the Isthmus of Rivas whose cacique Nicarao met Gil González Dávila 1522; conquered 1524.

polities.name: Chorotega Mangue
polities.note: Chorotega chiefdoms of the Pacific Nicaraguan lakes (Managua, Masaya, Diriangén of Diriamba).

polities.name: Nicoya
polities.note: Chorotega chiefdom of the Nicoya peninsula; allied with Spain 1523, absorbed into a Spanish corregimiento 1554.

polities.name: Matagalpa
polities.note: Misumalpan chiefdoms of the central Nicaraguan highlands.

polities.name: Huetar Kingdoms
polities.note: Two Huetar paramount chiefdoms of central Costa Rica (Garabito in the west, El Guarco under Correque in the east); conquered by Vázquez de Coronado 1561-1569.

polities.name: Talamanca
polities.note: Bribri and Cabécar chiefdoms that expelled Spanish missions (1610, 1709 Pablo Presbere revolt) and stayed independent; 19th-century 'kings of Talamanca' (Santiago Mayas, Antonio Saldaña to 1910).

polities.name: Ngäbe
polities.note: Largely unconquered mountain and Caribbean-slope people of western Panama.

polities.name: Coclé chiefdoms
polities.note: Gold-working chiefdoms of Coclé and Azuero (Natá, Parita/Paris, Escoria, Chirú); conquered by Espinosa 1516-1522.

polities.name: Urracá
polities.note: Veraguas cacique who fought the Spanish for nine years until his death c.1531.

polities.name: Cueva chiefdoms
polities.note: Chiefdoms of eastern Panama (Comogre, Careta, Pocorosa, Chepo) encountered by Balboa; destroyed by 1530.

polities.name: Guna
polities.note: Darién and San Blas people, allied with French/Scots/English against Spain; effectively independent through 1900 (1925 Tule Revolution).

polities.name: Bayano Maroons
polities.note: Maroon kingdom under King Bayano in eastern Panama; Bayano captured 1558, maroons allied with Drake 1572-73, peace settlements 1579-1582.

polities.name: Miskito Kingdom
polities.note: Miskito kingship allied with England (protectorate 1655-1787, 1844-1860); raided and took tribute from Spanish Central America; reduced to the Mosquito Reserve (Bluefields) 1860, annexed by Nicaragua 1894.

polities.name: Taíno cacicazgo of Marién
polities.note: NW Hispaniola cacicazgo of Guacanagarí, who hosted Columbus (La Navidad) 1492.

polities.name: Taíno cacicazgo of Maguá
polities.note: NE Hispaniola cacicazgo of Guarionex; subdued 1497.

polities.name: Taíno cacicazgo of Maguana
polities.note: Central Hispaniola cacicazgo of Caonabo, captured 1495.

polities.name: Taíno cacicazgo of Jaragua
polities.note: Largest cacicazgo, in SW Hispaniola; Anacaona executed after the Jaragua massacre 1503.

polities.name: Taíno cacicazgo of Higüey
polities.note: Eastern Hispaniola cacicazgo; war of 1503-1504, Cotubanamá executed.

polities.name: Bahoruco (Enriquillo)
polities.note: Taíno cacique Enriquillo held the Bahoruco mountains for 14 years; peace treaty with Spain 1533.

polities.name: Le Maniel
polities.note: Maroon community of the Bahoruco/Neiba border mountains; negotiated with French and Spanish authorities 1782-1785.

polities.name: Borikén
polities.note: Taíno cacicazgos of Puerto Rico under the paramount cacique Agüeybaná; revolt of 1511 crushed.

polities.name: Taíno cacicazgos of Cuba
polities.note: Some 29 cacicazgos of central and eastern Cuba (Baracoa, Bayamo, Camagüey, Sabaneque...); Hatuey burnt 1512, conquest by Velázquez complete 1514. Far western Cuba held Guanahatabey bands.

polities.name: Taíno Jamaica
polities.note: Taíno cacicazgos of Jamaica; Spanish settlement from 1509, population collapse by c.1520.

polities.name: Lucayan
polities.note: Taíno people of the Bahamas and Turks-Caicos; deported as slaves 1500-1513, islands depopulated.

polities.name: Kalinago
polities.note: Held the Lesser Antilles from Guadeloupe to Grenada; lost St Kitts, Guadeloupe, Martinique, Grenada, St Lucia to France/England 1625-1660; 1660 treaty left them Dominica and St Vincent; Dominica ceded to Britain 1763.

polities.name: Black Caribs of St Vincent
polities.note: Afro-Kalinago people of windward St Vincent under paramount chiefs (Joseph Chatoyer); fought Britain 1772-73 and 1795-96; deported to Roatán 1797.

polities.name: Leeward Maroons
polities.note: Cockpit Country maroons under Cudjoe; treaty with Britain 1739; Trelawny Town deported after the Second Maroon War 1796, Accompong remained.

polities.name: Windward Maroons
polities.note: Blue Mountains maroons led by Queen Nanny and Quao; treaty 1740; autonomous Moore Town and Charles Town persisted.

polities.name: Zipazgo of Bacatá
polities.note: Southern Muisca confederation of the zipa (Saguamanchica, Nemequene, Tisquesusa); conquered by Jiménez de Quesada 1537-1538. Seat Bacatá/Funza; Muequetá.

polities.name: Zacazgo of Hunza
polities.note: Northern Muisca confederation of the zaque (Quemuenchatocha, Aquiminzaque); taken 1537.

polities.name: Iraca
polities.note: Independent Muisca sacred province with the Sun Temple; burnt 1537.

polities.name: Tundama
polities.note: Northernmost independent Muisca chiefdom; cacique Tundama resisted until 1539.

polities.name: Guane
polities.note: Chibchan chiefdoms of the Mesa de los Santos (Santander); conquered by Martín Galeano 1540-1541.

polities.name: Chitarero
polities.note: Chibchan people around Pamplona; conquered 1549-1550.

polities.name: Lache
polities.note: Chibchan people of the Sierra Nevada del Cocuy.

polities.name: Muzo
polities.note: Carib-speaking emerald-country people west of the Muisca; resisted until c.1560.

polities.name: Panche
polities.note: Carib-speaking warriors of the Magdalena slope, enemies of the zipa; subdued by c.1575.

polities.name: Pijao
polities.note: Unconquered Central Cordillera people who raided Spanish settlements; defeated in Borja's war 1605-1612.

polities.name: Tairona
polities.note: Federation of towns of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta (Bonda, Pocigüeyca, Taironaka, Teyuna); resisted Santa Marta until the revolt of 1599-1600 was crushed; descendants Kogi, Arhuaco.

polities.name: Zenú
polities.note: Three-part Zenú realm (Finzenú, Panzenú, Zenúfana) of the Sinú and San Jorge basins; looted by Pedro de Heredia 1534-1536.

polities.name: Quimbaya
polities.note: Goldworking chiefdoms of the middle Cauca; conquered by Jorge Robledo 1539-1542.

polities.name: Pubenza
polities.note: Chiefdoms of the upper Cauca around Popayán; taken by Belalcázar 1536-1537.

polities.name: Pasto
polities.note: Andean chiefdoms of Nariño and Carchi on the Inca northern frontier; southern Pastos tributary to Huayna Capac c.1500.

polities.name: Wayuu
polities.note: Clan-based pastoral nation of the Guajira peninsula; adopted horses and cattle, traded with Dutch/English; defeated the 1769 Spanish campaign and remained self-governing through 1900.

polities.name: Barí
polities.note: Forest people of the Perijá range and Catatumbo who resisted colonisation into the 20th century.

polities.name: Caquetío
polities.note: Arawakan paramountcy of Falcón and the ABC islands under the diao Manaure; submitted to Ampíes 1527, then Welser rule from 1529.

polities.name: Timoto-Cuica
polities.note: Andean terrace-farming peoples of Mérida and Trujillo; conquered 1550s-1560.

polities.name: Cumanagoto
polities.note: Carib-speaking coastal people of NE Venezuela; Franciscan missions from the 1650s.

polities.name: Kariña
polities.note: Carib nation of the eastern llanos and lower Orinoco, allied to the Dutch slave trade; reduced by Catalan Capuchin and Franciscan missions 1720s-1740s.

polities.name: Warao
polities.note: Delta canoe people, largely outside colonial control.

polities.name: Achagua
polities.note: Arawakan llanos people; Jesuit Casanare/Meta missions from the 1660s.

polities.name: Kalina of the Guianas
polities.note: Carib coast nation from the Essequibo to Cayenne; fought the Dutch (1678-1686 Suriname war) and allied with them; leading Native power until c.1800.

polities.name: Lokono
polities.note: Arawakan people of the lower Guiana rivers (Berbice, Demerara, Suriname); Dutch allies and slave-catchers.

polities.name: Pemon-Makushi
polities.note: Carib-speaking savanna peoples of the Guiana Highlands; outside colonial rule until the late 19th century.

polities.name: Yanomami
polities.note: Uncontacted interfluvial people of the Parima/Siapa highlands throughout the period; no centralised polity.

polities.name: Saramaka
polities.note: Maroon nation formed from plantation escapees from c.1690; peace treaty with the Dutch 1762 recognising autonomy under a paramount chief (gaama).

polities.name: Ndyuka
polities.note: Maroon nation of the Cottica, Marowijne and Tapanahony rivers; treaty with the Dutch 1760; gaama seat at Diitabiki.

polities.name: Matawai
polities.note: Maroon group that split from the Saramaka; treaty with the Dutch 1767.

polities.name: Aluku
polities.note: Maroons under Boni who fought the Dutch (Boni Wars 1765-1793) then settled on the Lawa; status settled by Franco-Dutch accord 1860.

polities.name: Palenque de San Basilio
polities.note: Maroon town in the Montes de María founded by Benkos Biohó's followers; royal decree of freedom 1691/1713; self-governing.

polities.name: Esmeraldas Zambos
polities.note: Afro-indigenous polity founded by shipwrecked Africans under Alonso de Illescas; recognised by Quito as governors 1599-1600.

polities.name: Inca Empire
polities.note: Kingdom of Cusco (small valley state) until 1438 (first phase); expansion under Pachacuti (1438), Topa Inca (1471-1493) and Huayna Capac (1493-1527); civil war 1529-1532; Atahualpa captured at Cajamarca 1532, Cusco taken 1533. Eastern edge = Andean foothills; did not rule the Amazon lowlands.

polities.name: Neo-Inca State
polities.note: Rump Inca state founded by Manco Inca; seat Vitcos then Vilcabamba; ended with capture of Túpac Amaru 1572.

polities.name: Chimú
polities.note: North coast kingdom from Tumbes to the Chillón valley at its peak under Minchancaman; conquered by Topa Inca c.1470.

polities.name: Chincha Kingdom
polities.note: Maritime trading lordship; joined the Inca peacefully c.1476 and kept a privileged lord (the Lord of Chincha at Cajamarca 1532).

polities.name: Chanka Confederation
polities.note: Rivals of Cusco whose attack (c.1438) was repelled by Pachacuti, launching Inca expansion.

polities.name: Ychsma
polities.note: Lordship of the Rímac and Lurín valleys around the oracle of Pachacamac; absorbed by the Inca c.1470.

polities.name: Cuismancu
polities.note: Northern highland kingdom allied with Chimor; conquered by Topa Inca c.1463.

polities.name: Huanca Confederation
polities.note: Mantaro valley chiefdoms (Hatun Xauxa, Lurinhuanca, Ananhuanca); conquered c.1460, later Spanish allies.

polities.name: Chachapoya
polities.note: Cloud-forest confederation subdued by Topa Inca c.1475; repeatedly rebelled, sided with Spain.

polities.name: Colla Kingdom
polities.note: Aymara kingdom NW of Lake Titicaca; defeated by Pachacuti c.1450-1460.

polities.name: Lupaca Kingdom
polities.note: Aymara kingdom on the SW Titicaca shore with Pacific coast colonies; Inca vassal after c.1460, retained its lords.

polities.name: Pacajes
polities.note: Aymara lordship south of Lake Titicaca; Inca vassal after c.1460.

polities.name: Charcas Confederation
polities.note: Aymara federation (Qaraqara, Charka, Chuy, Chicha) of north Potosí; Inca allies/vassals from the 1470s.

polities.name: Cañari
polities.note: Highland Ecuador confederation conquered by Topa Inca c.1470; Tomebamba became an Inca capital; Cañari later allied with Spain.

polities.name: Puruhá
polities.note: Chiefdoms of Chimborazo province, annexed by the Inca.

polities.name: Caranqui-Cayambe Confederation
polities.note: Northern Ecuador chiefdoms (Caranqui, Cayambe, Otavalo, Cochasquí, with the Quitu) that resisted Huayna Capac until the Yahuarcocha massacre c.1495-1500. The 'Kingdom of Quito' of Velasco is legendary.

polities.name: Manteño-Huancavilca
polities.note: Seafaring merchant league of coastal Ecuador with the island lordship of Puná; never fully conquered by the Inca.

polities.name: Omaguaca
polities.note: Quebrada de Humahuaca chiefdoms; Inca subjects c.1480-1533; resisted Spain under Viltipoco until 1594-1595.

polities.name: Atacameño
polities.note: Oasis communities of the Atacama puna; Inca-ruled from c.1470, fortress of Quitor taken by Spain 1540, final submission 1557.

polities.name: Diaguita-Calchaquí
polities.note: Diaguita chiefdoms of the Calchaquí valleys; Inca vassals c.1480-1533; fought Spain in the Calchaquí Wars (1560-1563, 1630-1643, 1658-1667) before deportation.

polities.name: Quilmes
polities.note: Fortified Diaguita town of c.5,000 people; last to fall in the third Calchaquí war; deported to Buenos Aires 1667.

polities.name: Chilean Diaguita
polities.note: Valley chiefdoms of Copiapó, Huasco, Elqui, Limarí and Choapa under Inca rule c.1470-1536, then Spain.

polities.name: Picunche
polities.note: Northern Mapudungun-speakers of central Chile; Inca-ruled to the Maipo/Maule c.1470-1536; Michimalonco attacked Santiago 1541.

polities.name: Huarpe
polities.note: Lagoon-farming people of Cuyo; Inca influence to c.1533; encomienda after the founding of Mendoza 1561 and San Juan 1562.

polities.name: Comechingón
polities.note: Hill peoples of Córdoba (with the Sanavirón to the NE); subjected after the founding of Córdoba 1573.

polities.name: Mapuche of Araucanía
polities.note: Lof and ayllarewe alliances grouped into four butalmapus; destroyed the Spanish southern cities after Curalaba (1598); Biobío frontier recognised at the parlamentos of Quilín (1641) onward; independent until the Chilean Occupation of Araucanía 1861-1883 (Villarrica 1883). No permanent capital (Purén/Angol are emblematic). The Kingdom of Araucanía and Patagonia (1860-62) was a French adventurer's claim, not a governing polity.

polities.name: Huilliche
polities.note: Southern Mapuche (with the Cunco) who destroyed Osorno 1600 and stayed independent between Valdivia (refounded 1645) and Chiloé; ceded land by the Parliament of Las Canoas 1793, Osorno refounded 1796.

polities.name: Pehuenche
polities.note: Araucaria-gathering mountain people on both sides of the Andes; Spanish allies from 1760s parlamentos; subdued 1880s.

polities.name: Salinas Grandes Confederation
polities.note: Mapuche-led Pampas confederation founded by Calfucurá after the Masallé massacre (1834); controlled the salt-and-cattle trade, raided Bahía Blanca (1859) and received Argentine rations; under Namuncurá from 1873; broken by the Conquest of the Desert 1879, Namuncurá surrendered 1884.

polities.name: Ranquel Ulmanate
polities.note: Ranquel confederation of the Mamuel Mapu (caldén forest) between the Desaguadero-Salado and western Buenos Aires province, north to the Quinto river; leaders Yanquetruz, Painé, Mariano Rosas (Panguitruz Güer), Baigorrita; conquered 1879.

polities.name: Boroganos
polities.note: Mapuche migrants from Boroa who settled at Salinas Grandes; destroyed by Calfucurá at Masallé 1834.

polities.name: Manzaneros
polities.note: Mapuche-Tehuelche lordship of the Neuquén-Limay apple country led by Valentín Sayhueque, who styled it a government; surrendered 1885.

polities.name: Querandí
polities.note: Pampas hunters who besieged first Buenos Aires (1536-1541); dispersed after the second founding 1580.

polities.name: Pampas Tehuelche
polities.note: Hunting bands of the southern Pampas and northern Patagonia (Río Negro), progressively Mapuchised after 1700; defeated 1879-1880.

polities.name: Aónikenk
polities.note: Horse-riding hunting nation of Patagonia between the Chubut and the Strait of Magellan; caciques such as Casimiro Biguá dealt with Chile and Argentina; overrun by Argentine campaigns 1883-1885.

polities.name: Selkʼnam
polities.note: Hunter nation of Isla Grande de Tierra del Fuego organised in haruwen territories; destroyed by ranchers and gold-seekers 1880s-1900s.

polities.name: Yaghan
polities.note: Canoe people of the Beagle Channel and Cape Horn islands.

polities.name: Kawésqar
polities.note: Canoe nomads of the western Patagonian channels.

polities.name: Chono
polities.note: Canoe people between Chiloé and the Taitao peninsula; removed to Chiloé missions by the late 18th century.

polities.name: Charrúa
polities.note: Horse nation of the Banda Oriental and Entre Ríos (with Minuán/Guenoa); resisted Spain and Portugal, allied with Artigas; massacred at Salsipuedes by the Uruguayan state 1831.

polities.name: Chaná
polities.note: Fishing peoples of the lower Paraná and Uruguay islands.

polities.name: Guaraní chiefdoms
polities.note: Village federations (tekoha/guará) of the Paraguay, Paraná and Uruguay basins; Carió allied with Spain at Asunción 1537 under the encomienda; remaining groups gathered into Jesuit reductions from 1609.

polities.name: Jesuit Reductions of the Guaraní
polities.note: Self-governing Guaraní mission towns under Jesuit administration and their own militia; Guairá and Itatín missions abandoned after bandeirante raids (1628-1631) and concentrated on the Paraná-Uruguay; seven eastern towns ceded to Portugal 1750 (Guaraní War 1754-56); Jesuits expelled 1767-68.

polities.name: Chiquitos Missions
polities.note: Ten Jesuit mission towns of the Chiquitano lowlands, autonomous under the Audiencia of Charcas; before 1691 independent Chiquitano villages occupied the same area.

polities.name: Mojeño chiefdoms
polities.note: Arawakan raised-field and mound-building chiefdoms (Mojo, Baure) of the Beni savannas; reorganised as missions from 1682.

polities.name: Moxos Missions
polities.note: Some 24 Jesuit mission towns of the Beni; Jesuits expelled 1767.

polities.name: Maynas Missions
polities.note: Jesuit mission province of the upper Amazon, Marañón, Huallaga and Napo among Mainas, Cocama, Omagua and others; contested with Portuguese Carmelites; Jesuits expelled 1768.

polities.name: Chiriguano
polities.note: Guaraní-speaking nation of the Andean piedmont that held off the Inca and Spain (defeated Viceroy Toledo 1574); Franciscan missions from the 1760s; independence ended at Kuruyuki 1892.

polities.name: Qom
polities.note: Horse-raiding Guaycuruan nation of the central Chaco between the Pilcomayo and Bermejo; independent until the Argentine Chaco campaigns of 1884 and 1911.

polities.name: Wichí
polities.note: Mataco-Mataguayan fishing and foraging bands of the western Chaco rivers; outside colonial rule.

polities.name: Mocoví
polities.note: Guaycuruan horse nation raiding Santa Fe and Santiago del Estero; Jesuit reduction of San Javier 1743; last revolt 1904.

polities.name: Abipón
polities.note: Guaycuruan horse people described by Dobrizhoffer; missions San Jerónimo 1748 and others; dispersed by c.1800.

polities.name: Mbayá-Guaicurú
polities.note: Equestrian Guaycuruan nobility ruling Guaná (Chané) serfs on both banks of the upper Paraguay; peace treaty with Portugal 1791; descendants Kadiwéu.

polities.name: Payaguá
polities.note: Canoe-warrior nation controlling the Paraguay river; attacked Portuguese monsoon convoys 1720s-1730s; settled at Asunción from 1740.

polities.name: Nivaclé and Chorote
polities.note: Mataco-Mataguayan peoples of the middle Pilcomayo, unconquered through 1900.

polities.name: Ayoreo
polities.note: Zamucoan forest people of the northern Chaco, briefly in Chiquitos missions (1720s) but otherwise uncontacted until the 20th century.

polities.name: Kaingang
polities.note: Jê people of the southern Brazilian plateau; resisted Portuguese expansion (Guarapuava 1810, Palmas 1840s) until settled in aldeamentos.

polities.name: Xokleng
polities.note: Jê forest people of the Santa Catarina escarpment, attacked by bugreiros in the late 19th century.

polities.name: Carijó
polities.note: Guaraní coastal people from Cananéia to the Lagoa dos Patos; depopulated by São Paulo slave raids by the 1640s.

polities.name: Tamoio Confederation
polities.note: Tupinambá alliance from Cabo Frio to Bertioga led by Cunhambebe and Aimberê, allied with France Antarctique; truce of Iperoig 1563; defeated with the fall of Uruçumirim 1567.

polities.name: Tupinambá of Rio and Cabo Frio
polities.note: Tupinambá villages of Guanabara and Cabo Frio before and after the Tamoio Confederation; Cabo Frio Tupinambá destroyed 1575.

polities.name: Tupinambá of Bahia
polities.note: Tupinambá of the Bay of All Saints and Recôncavo; defeated by Governor Mem de Sá 1558-1560s.

polities.name: Tupinambá of Maranhão
polities.note: Tupinambá migrants of Maranhão and eastern Pará; allied with France Équinoxiale 1612-1615; subdued after the Portuguese founding of Belém 1616 and the 1617-1619 revolts.

polities.name: Tupiniquim
polities.note: Tupi coast people of Porto Seguro-Espírito Santo (and separately São Vicente), early Portuguese allies; absorbed into Jesuit aldeias.

polities.name: Caeté
polities.note: Tupi people of southern Pernambuco and Alagoas who killed Bishop Sardinha 1556; declared enemies and enslaved 1562.

polities.name: Potiguara
polities.note: Tupi nation of Paraíba and Rio Grande do Norte allied with French traders; peace with Portugal 1599; later split during the Dutch war (Poti/Camarão vs Pedro Poti).

polities.name: Tabajara
polities.note: Tupi people of the Ibiapaba range and Ceará; Jesuit mission of Ibiapaba 1656.

polities.name: Tarairiú
polities.note: Non-Tupi (Tapuia) nations of the sertão under King Janduí, allies of Dutch Brazil (1630-1654); fought the Guerra dos Bárbaros 1683-1713.

polities.name: Goitacá
polities.note: Feared non-Tupi people of the Paraíba do Sul delta; defeated the donatary of São Tomé (1546); dispersed by the 1630s.

polities.name: Aimoré-Botocudo
polities.note: Macro-Jê forest nation of the Atlantic hinterland between Bahia and Minas; blocked the coast in the 16th century; target of the 1808 'just war'; subdued by the 1880s.

polities.name: Kayapó
polities.note: Northern Kayapó of the Xingu-Araguaia; Southern Kayapó of Goiás/Triângulo fought Portuguese miners in the 18th century and were nearly extinct by 1900.

polities.name: Akwẽ (Xavante-Xerente)
polities.note: Jê nations of Goiás and Tocantins; part settled in aldeias (Carretão) 1788, Xavante migrated west to the Rio das Mortes c.1820s-1860s and stayed independent.

polities.name: Bororo
polities.note: Jê people of the Mato Grosso plateau; Western Bororo allied to Portuguese, Eastern Bororo fought settlers until 1880s.

polities.name: Mundurukú
polities.note: Warrior nation of the Tapajós that expanded in the 1770s; peace with Portugal 1795, then auxiliaries; largely autonomous through 1900.

polities.name: Mura
polities.note: Riverine raiders of the Madeira and lower Purus who attacked Portuguese traffic until their peace of 1784-1786.

polities.name: Omagua
polities.note: Tupi-Guaraní riverine chiefdoms along 700 km of the Amazon (Solimões) seen by Orellana 1542 and Ursúa 1560; reduced by Jesuit Samuel Fritz's missions and Portuguese slaving by c.1710.

polities.name: Machiparo
polities.note: Populous riverine chiefdom met by Orellana's expedition 1542 below the Omagua; vanished by the 17th century.

polities.name: Tapajó
polities.note: Paramount chiefdom at the Tapajós-Amazon confluence (Santarém culture); Jesuit mission 1661, population wiped out by slaving and epidemics.

polities.name: Manao
polities.note: Arawakan trading nation of the Rio Negro; under Ajuricaba allied with the Dutch and fought Portugal 1723-1728.

polities.name: Nheengaíba
polities.note: Aruã and other 'Nheengaíba' nations of Marajó and the Amazon mouth who fought the Portuguese until the peace brokered by António Vieira 1659.

polities.name: Shuar
polities.note: Jivaroan nations who repelled the Inca and destroyed Spanish Logroño and Sevilla del Oro in the 1599 revolt; independent through 1900.

polities.name: Asháninka
polities.note: Arawakan nation of the central selva; Franciscan missions expelled by the Juan Santos Atahualpa rising 1742-1756, after which the Gran Pajonal stayed outside Spanish/Peruvian rule until the 1847 refounding of San Ramón and the Perené colony (1890s).

polities.name: Shipibo-Conibo
polities.note: Panoan river nations of the Ucayali; killed missionaries in 1698 and 1766 revolts; autonomous through most of the period.

polities.name: Palmares
polities.note: Maroon kingdom in the hills of Alagoas/Pernambuco under Ganga Zumba and Zumbi; resisted Dutch and Portuguese expeditions; capital Macaco fell 1694, Zumbi killed 1695.

polities.name: Quilombo do Quariterê
polities.note: Maroon community near Vila Bela in Mato Grosso ruled by Queen Tereza de Benguela; destroyed 1770, re-formed and destroyed again 1795.

polities.name: Quilombo do Campo Grande
polities.note: Large federation of maroon settlements in western Minas Gerais; destroyed by expeditions 1746 and 1759.

gaps.area: Colonial lands generally (New Spain, Guatemala, New Granada, Peru, Río de la Plata, Brazil, Caribbean colonies) and post-1810 republics
gaps.note: Deliberately not listed: this file covers Native, maroon and mission polities only. Once a Native entry ends (to-year), its land passes to the colonial/republican state already in the base dataset.
Foraging Guanahatabey bands with no known chiefdom; no polity.

gaps.area: Atacama desert core and high puna salt flats
gaps.note: Effectively uninhabited between oases; only Atacameño oasis lordships.

gaps.area: Upper Rio Negro, Vaupés and Caquetá-Putumayo interfluves (Tukanoan and Arawakan groups)
gaps.note: Many small clan-based peoples (Tukano, Baniwa, Witoto); none mapped individually. Thin coverage.

gaps.area: Juruá-Purus and upper Madeira basins (Kashinawa, Apurinã, Paumari, Tupi-Kawahib)
gaps.note: Village-level peoples outside any state until the rubber boom (1870s-1900); not listed individually.

gaps.area: Upper Xingu and western Mato Grosso (Xinguano chiefdoms, Paresí, Nambikwara)
gaps.note: Xinguano regional chiefdoms (Kuikuro) and Paresí existed but lack datable territorial records; not listed.

gaps.area: Central Brazilian sertão of Bahia/Minas (Kiriri, Kamakã, Pataxó, Akroá)
gaps.note: Tapuia peoples between the coast and the São Francisco; only Aimoré-Botocudo and Tarairiú are listed.
Mobile groups; only Achagua listed. Jesuit/Capuchin Orinoco missions (1680s-1767) not listed separately.

gaps.area: Interior Guiana forests south of the maroon belt (Trio, Wayana, Waiwai)
gaps.note: Small Carib-speaking groups without recorded polities.

gaps.area: Northern Mexican fringe 21-23N east of the Sierra Madre Occidental (Zacatecos)
gaps.note: Zacateco bands not listed; partly covered by Guachichil and Caxcan.
